pass_a_gloss: [...] the axe lies at the root of the trees; every tree then not making good fruit is cut out and thrown into fire. Israel then having unbridled the increase toward the need to offend, and being devoted, as I said just now, to the false worships of the idols, God foreshows through the prophet the capture of Jerusalem that will be in its times, and says: [Lemma, Isaiah 22:1-2:] What happened to you now, that you all went up onto vain housetops? The city was filled with those shouting; your wounded, not wounded of sword, nor your dead, dead of war. It seems then to show here the ravaging in the times of Jeconiah, and to blame greatly those from Israel, as not knowing even in the evils themselves, and in misfortunes so very much at their peak, to achieve what leads to benefit, and what was going to be for them a procurer of the favour from above. For it was needed that, weeping and lamenting, they go up into the house of God, and announce the change of mind, and ask forgetting of the outrages they had committed, and seek the helping hand from him and alone. And this he himself taught, saying through one of the holy prophets: Gird yourselves and beat [your breasts], priests, lament, those ministering to the altar, go in, sleep in sackcloths, those ministering to God, because sacrifice and libation are withheld from your house; sanctify a fast, proclaim a service, gather elders, all dwelling in the land, into the house of your God, and cry to the Lord earnestly, Alas, alas, for the day. These things then it was needed that, doing, they appease the one who has power to save, having been provoked. But they did not, perhaps, even receive into mind that it is fitting to do these things, but went up to the highest parts of the houses, and there were beatings of the breast everywhere, and laments of children, consumed perhaps by hunger and thirst. For these things must happen to the besieged among cities. For this reason he says: What happened to you now, that you all went up onto vain housetops? For why, he says, even in fears so unbearable, and when the words for you were about the last things, and the whole contest, did you not cry to God, but rather leapt up onto housetops, although the thing profited you nothing? For because of this he says also vain housetops. Why also was the city filled with those shouting? Not, surely, rather toward God, but crying at random, and all but very much distressed at the evils that had come inside the doors. It was needed that the lament be for change of mind; it was needed that the tear be poured down toward God. Behold, he says, before touching battle, before taking hold of a sword, before practising resistance, the city has become full of dead. Useful then [the section breaks off].
pass_b_english: … “the axe lies at the root of the trees; every tree, then, that does not bear good fruit is cut down and thrown into the fire” (Matthew 3:10).

Since Israel, then, gave free rein to its advance in sin, and was devoted, as I said just now, to the false worship of idols, God through the prophet foretells the capture of Jerusalem that would come in its time, and says: “What has happened to you now, that you have all gone up to useless housetops? The city is filled with people shouting. Your wounded are not wounded by the sword, nor are your dead the dead of war” (Isaiah 22:1–2).

It seems to point here to the devastation in the days of Jeconiah, and to accuse those of Israel severely, because even amid these very evils, in misfortunes at their very height, they did not know how to do what leads to their good and what would win them favor from above. For they ought to have gone up to the house of God weeping and lamenting, to promise repentance, to ask pardon for the outrages they had committed, and to seek the helping hand from him, and from him alone.

And he himself taught this, saying through one of the holy prophets: “Gird yourselves and beat your breasts, you priests; wail, you who minister at the altar. Go in, sleep in sackcloth, you who minister to God, for sacrifice and drink offering are withheld from your house. Sanctify a fast, proclaim a solemn service, gather the elders, all who dwell in the land, into the house of your God, and cry out earnestly to the Lord: Alas, alas, for the day” (Joel 1:13–15).

These are the things they ought to have done to appease the one who has power to save, since he had been provoked. But it seems that they did not even let it enter their minds that they ought to do these things. Instead they went up to the highest parts of their houses, and everywhere there were laments, and the wailing of children, wasting away, it may be, from hunger and thirst. For such things must happen to cities under siege.

That is why he says: “What has happened to you now, that you have all gone up to useless housetops?” Why, he says, even amid terrors so unbearable, when your peril had reached its last extremity and everything was at stake, did you not cry out to God, but instead leapt up to the housetops, though that did you no good at all? That is why he calls them useless housetops.

And why was the city filled with people shouting? Not, surely, people crying to God, but people crying out at random, and all but beside themselves at the evils that had come within their doors. The lament ought to have been for repentance; the tears ought to have been shed before God. See, he says: before you joined battle, before you took up the sword, before you planned any resistance, the city became full of dead. It is useful, then, …

choices.english: gave free rein to its advance in sin
choices.why: Israel lets its progress in sin run unbridled; it is not 'hardened and recently devoted'.
The prophet blames them for not knowing how to act rightly even in their worst troubles.
rejected: as they blame, knowing what is to come

choices.why: Cyril explains μάταια: going up to the roofs did them no good.
The object is God, who had been provoked and has power to save.
μετάγνωσις, change of mind, is the turning they ought to have shown.
